title: Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59
description: Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta, whose credits include the crime thriller “Kaante,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-sta
body:
Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta, whose credits include the crime thriller “Kaante,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-starring “Kaabil,” has died following a fall at his Mumbai residence on Oct. 30. He was 59, according to the Press Trust of India.

	Director Milap Zaveri, a longtime friend of Gupta who worked on the dialogue for “Kaante,” confirmed the death to PTI. “It is true that he passed away. He fell and hit his head,” Zaveri said.
	

	Police in Mumbai’s Versova neighborhood have filed an accidental death report. Deputy Commissioner of Police Purushottam Karad told the Free Press Journal that members of Gupta’s family were sleeping when the incident occurred and became aware of it the following morning. “The family has not raised any suspicion or lodged a complaint,” Karad said.

	Gupta was a prominent exponent of the glossy, action-driven Hindi-language crime thriller, bringing a visual sensibility heavily indebted to Hollywood to an industry traditionally dominated by melodrama and musicals. His career behind the camera began with “Aatish: Feel the Fire” in 1994, featuring Sanjay Dutt and Aditya Pancholi. He subsequently directed “Ram Shastra,” “Jung” and “Khauff,” developing an enduring professional relationship with Dutt that extended across 10 films, including projects Gupta produced.

	The filmmaker achieved one of his biggest successes with “Kaante” in 2002, assembling Amitabh Bachchan, Dutt, Suniel Shetty, Mahesh Manjrekar, Lucky Ali and Kumar Gaurav for a Los Angeles-set heist thriller about a group of criminals planning a bank robbery. The production was filming in the city when the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, forced changes to its location schedule, as Gupta recounted in a Rediff interview the following year.
	

	The film’s similarities to Quentin Tarantino‘s “Reservoir Dogs” drew considerable attention, although Tarantino subsequently expressed admiration for “Kaante” in a 2007 interview covered by the Times of India. Gupta received a Filmfare nomination for best director.

	Questions about the influence of international films followed Gupta throughout his career, and he made little secret of his willingness to draw inspiration from existing material. Responding to accusations of plagiarism in his 2002 Rediff interview, he said he would “beg, borrow and steal from any medium” in pursuit of a compelling story.

	Several of his subsequent films reflected that philosophy. “Musafir” (2004) bore similarities to Oliver Stone’s “U Turn,” while the Dutt and John Abraham thriller “Zinda” (2006) attracted particular controversy over its resemblance to Park Chan-wook’s South Korean film “Oldboy.” The Korean production company Show East told Star News in November 2005 that it was considering legal remedies should the completed Hindi film prove substantially similar to the original. Gupta later directed “Jazbaa” (2015), an adaptation of the Korean thriller “Seven Days” that brought Aishwarya Rai Bachchan back to the screen.

	Gupta also established himself as a producer through White Feather Films. The company’s credits included “Shootout at Lokhandwala” (2007), “Acid Factory,” “Pankh” and the anthology “Dus Kahaniyaan,” which Gupta also directed. He returned to the gangster genre with “Shootout at Wadala” (2013), a prequel to “Shootout at Lokhandwala” drawing on S. Hussain Zaidi’s nonfiction book “Dongri to Dubai.”

	With “Kaabil” in 2017, Gupta directed Hrithik Roshan as a visually impaired man pursuing vengeance, in a film produced by Rakesh Roshan. His later work included the crime drama “Mumbai Saga” (2021), a T-Series co-production whose theatrical prospects were affected by a renewed surge in COVID-19 infections. His producing credits also extended to “Visfot” (2024), a Hindi adaptation of the Venezuelan thriller “Rock, Paper, Scissors.”

	Colleagues remembered Gupta’s contributions to the industry’s visual and promotional vocabulary. “Raees” director Rahul Dholakia described him on X as a stylish filmmaker and “maybe the first to present trailers and cut promos to pitch the film idea to actors and distributors.” 
	

	Director Kunal Kohli, whose films include “Fanaa,” recalled a conversation with Gupta only a few weeks before his death, as well as their time together as members of an awards jury. “You had many more films and many years to go,” Kohli wrote.

	Dutt posted: “Gupts, my brother. I still cannot believe that you are gone. We have shared so much together, so many memories and so many years of friendship. You have always been family to me, and that will never change. I will miss you, our conversations and all the times we spent together.”

	Sound designer Resul Pookutty, Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” wrote: “What a terrible and shocking news for me personally and our friends and family. 25 Years of working together. I’m not able to process this… we will miss you, one of the sanest voices from mainstream Hindi cinema… May your soul rest in eternal peace.” 

	Beyond filmmaking, Gupta maintained an active presence on X, frequently offering pointed commentary on the Hindi film industry’s creative and commercial direction. He had also begun discussing a possible return to one of his best-known properties. Following the resolution of a dispute involving White Feather Films and Pritish Nandy Communications over “Kaante,” Gupta revealed on the “InControversial” podcast earlier this year that he had developed the foundations of a sequel.

	He said the story for “Kaante 2” had been worked out “at a very base level” and that he intended to begin writing the screenplay.

	Gupta is survived by his wife and two children.

schema.headline: Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59

title: Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass
description: The Tokyo International Film Festival’s Tokyo Talk program presented a masterclass with Zeze Takahisa, director of the festival’s opening film, “Su
body:
The Tokyo International Film Festival’s Tokyo Talk program presented a masterclass with Zeze Takahisa, director of the festival’s opening film, “Sukiyaki.” 

	Held before a full-house crowd at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, the talk focused on Zeze’s early “pink” (softcore porn) and indie films, followed by questions about his more recent work.

	Born in 1960 in Oita Prefecture, Zeze joined a pink film production company in 1986 and worked as an assistant director. He made his directorial debut in 1989 with “Extracurricular Activity: Rape,” for which he won the Pink Grand Prix Award for Best New Director. Together with Sano Kazuhiro, Sato Toshiki and Sato Hisayasu, Zeze was hailed as one of the “Four Heavenly Kings of Pink.”
	

	Pink films screened in specialized theaters for an exclusively male audience, and directors had to insert a bed scene every 10 minutes or so. “I’ve always been pretty firm in my convictions,” said Zeze. “Starting from the early 1990s the culture shifted and I had more freedom to say what I wanted. That kind of thing was important to me.”

	At the time, Zeze was interested in stories about female criminals. “It’s just different from the male perspective,” he said. “The motives behind the crimes and so on. I found it fascinating.”

	Scripted by Zeze, “Extracurricular Activity: Rape” was about delinquent high school girls who hang out at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and battle the yakuza. Zeze gave it the “private” title “Go to Haneda and You Will See Kids Dressed Like Pirates Ready to Attack.”
	

	Asked about a 1994 pink, “Genuine Lesbians: Embarrassing Positions” (Zeze’s own title: “Fallen Angels in September”), Zeze said the film, which was about female soulmates, reflected the interest he described as “this whole mysticism thing” shared by many young people then. “Searching for past lives became a sort of trend, and people started seeking connections to this different world,” he added. “I thought that maybe I could make a movie centered around something like that.”

	Zeze said the “Four Heavenly Kings” moniker came from a pink theater “in Toyama – or maybe Ishikawa – I can’t remember.” It reminded Zeze and the other “kings” of “Nouvelle Vague” – a tag that gave critical and commercial cachet to its members. “So we figured that, rather than work as individuals, we should debut under a group name,” he said. “We decided to use the ‘Four Heavenly Kings’ label to our advantage.”

	The “kings” films were also shown in retrospectives at the Rotterdam festival and elsewhere abroad. “Actually, the overseas reception came first, and then it was sort of re-imported” back to Japan, Zeze said.

	Meanwhile, in Japan, the “kings” and other pink film directors still had to incorporate a certain amount of eros. “No one was telling us to stop doing these politically sensitive things,” said Zeze. “It was just wonderful… there really was a lot of freedom back then.”

	Also, pink film directors were not confined to a porn ghetto. “Things weren’t standardized back then,” Zeze said. “I worked with directors from my generation who had diverse backgrounds, like Aoyama Shinji and Suzuki Takuji. We’d get together either because we’d met by chance or because we wanted to create something interesting.”

	In 1997 Zeze made his mainstream debut with the teen horror “Kokkuri-san” but continued to alternate between pink and mainstream films for the next decade.

	In 2010 he released his most ambitious film to date, “Heaven’s Story,” a 278-minute revenge drama that screened in the Forum section of the Berlin Film Festival, where it won the FIPRESCI Prize.

	“It was different from a so-called ‘ordinary movie,’” Zeze said. “I’d been working on commercial films until then, but I realized I had to do something else. Personally, I felt a sense of urgency – or maybe a sense of crisis – that things weren’t going well, and that’s what pushed me to take on this challenge.”
	

	There’s a lot of talk, Zeze said, about how difficult it is to make a film unless it’s adapted from source material. “But the movies we actually found interesting or the ones I personally found entertaining were all originals.”

	Zeze himself has made commercial films with stories sourced from existing IP, such as the hit 2016 two-part mystery/suspense “64,” which was based on a bestselling novel, but said, “The industry is too focused on the ‘source material market.’ They think that if the source material is selling well, they should adapt it.”

	“So I feel that pursuing original concepts and making original films is incredibly important right now,” he added. “They have a unique, compelling strength.”

schema.headline: Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass

title: Japan’s Film Funds Look Beyond Production Committees to Build New Financing Models
description: Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the i
body:
Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the industry. But it can also cap budgets at what the industry itself can raise, make it harder for overseas investors to take part and slow decisions when every rights holder must agree. 

	At a panel at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, speakers examined whether film funds can ease those limits while still fitting Japan’s market.
	

	“Film Funds in Japan: What Works, What Doesn’t, and What Comes Next” featured Kii Muneyuki, CEO and producer of K2 Pictures, which works with filmmakers including Kore-eda Hirokazu, Miike Takashi and Nishikawa Miwa; Ibe Tomonobu, CEO of Questry, a Tokyo startup that uses digital securities to fund anime and other Japanese content; Nakagawa Keita, managing director at MUFG Bank; and Motoyanagi Yusuke, partner at law firm Nishimura & Asahi. 

	Kii presented K2P Film Fund I as one example of a new structure. The fund closed in February at about JPY5 billion ($32 million) and aims to back around 50 films over seven years. It is a blind pool, meaning investors commit money before the films are chosen. Its investors include MUFG, the Development Bank of Japan and other financial institutions and companies, and a greenlight committee oversees project approvals. Kii said five films had been released in theaters in 2026.

	Kii said a central question for film funds is how to return revenue to creators, including income from streaming and other windows after a film’s theatrical run. He also said it is hard to rely on overseas box office, and that Japanese companies need to build businesses beyond distribution.
	

	The panel compared financing structures in the U.S. and South Korea. In the U.S., producers combine presales with completion guarantees to help secure bank loans. A completion guarantee covers delivery of a film on budget and on schedule, rather than its commercial performance. South Korea relies on public-private support, with government-backed guarantees helping projects get bank financing.

	Nakagawa presented a Japan-specific feasibility study commissioned by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. MUFG was selected to carry it out on March 31. Running through February 2027, the study will use real-world data to develop valuation and completion-guarantee models, and test the full process from application and review to contract drafting. The study assesses feasibility and does not guarantee that financing or completion guarantees will become available.

	The discussion closed with four priorities: regulation, capital, creators and cross-border business. These include clarifying which regulations should be expanded and when, combining debt with subsidies and completion guarantees, and building creator returns into fund structures. Speakers also pointed to language and tax hurdles to cross-border investment, including “permanent establishment” rules that can make international investors liable for Japanese tax.

schema.headline: Japan’s Film Funds Look Beyond Production Committees to Build New Financing Models

title: Bill Maher Fact-Checks Kid Rock After He Compares Abdul El-Sayed to 9/11 Hijackers on ‘Real Time’
description: Bill Maher opened his new episode of “Real Time” Friday night by addressing Trump’s 1,300-word social media tirade against him following their Whit
body:
Bill Maher opened his new episode of “Real Time” Friday night by addressing Trump’s 1,300-word social media tirade against him following their White House dinner earlier this month, with the comic comparing the president to Taylor Swift.

	Following a sit-down interview with Republican Senator Ted Cruz, who was busy hawking his new book on Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, Maher welcomed his panel — Jim VandeHei, the co-founder and CEO of Axios, and Kid Rock, a singer who once rapped, “Young ladies, young ladies, I like ‘em underage, see / Some say that’s statutory — but I say it’s mandatory.”
	

	Kid Rock was present at that Oct. 15 White House dinner with Trump, Maher and ESPN pundit Stephen A Smith, and appeared to defend Maher against Trump’s series of claims in his record-breaking Truth Social post.

	“He said I was drunk. I was not drunk,” claimed Maher, to which Kid Rock replied, “You were pretty high.” “We had a good time — and it was four hours, right?” asked Maher. “We had a good time,” offered Kid Rock, adding, “I had to leave early, but yes, it was… Was he talking about dinner or the whole thing?”

	After their exchange over the White House dinner, Maher brought up how former president Obama campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, who is Muslim. Maher said, “As far as this issue goes about Islam in America and candidates who are Muslim, the left is naïve and the right is hysterical.” He then quoted Trump, who said of El-Sayed, “If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and welcome hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
	

	“You don’t really believe that,” Maher questioned Kid Rock, who grew up on a sprawling estate in the suburbs of Michigan. Kid Rock subsequently compared El -Sayed to the 9/11 hijackers, saying, “People talk about assimilation too all the time, right? This man very much has assimilated — good education, well-spoken, even a good-looking guy — [but] you know who else assimilated very well? Those pieces of shit that flew those planes into our World Trade Centers. The Fort Hood shooter. This has happened all over the world, so it scares the hell out of me, this Islamic extremism. I don’t know, is he a wolf in sheep’s clothing, or is he just a wolf in a wolf’s clothing?”

	Maher replied, “Not that it matters so much, but the 9/11 hijackers weren’t here assimilated. They were from Saudi Arabia.”

	“The ones who flew the planes were from Saudi Arabia? No,” Kid Rock shot back.

	In fact, 15 of the 19 9/11 hijackers were from Saudi Arabia, two were from the United Arab Emirates, one was from Egypt and one was from Lebanon, and the first hijackers to arrive in the U.S. came in January of 2000, so they weren’t “assimilated very well,” as the man formerly known as Robert James Ritchie so boldly claimed.

schema.headline: Bill Maher Fact-Checks Kid Rock After He Compares Abdul El-Sayed to 9/11 Hijackers on ‘Real Time’

title: Japan’s New 2027 Anime Award Should Put Creators in the Spotlight, Industry Leaders Say at Tokyo Market
description: A new Japanese anime award planned for 2027 should put the people who make anime in the spotlight, industry leaders said at TIFFCOM, the market of
body:
A new Japanese anime award planned for 2027 should put the people who make anime in the spotlight, industry leaders said at TIFFCOM, the market of the Tokyo International Film Festival.

	The session was moderated by Fujitsu Ryota, programming advisor for the festival’s animation section. Shimizu Akira, a director of the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), is president and representative director of A-1 Pictures. He was joined by Studio Chizu president Saito Yuichiro, producer of “The Girl Who Leapt Through Time,” “Summer Wars” and “Wolf Children,” and Saito Masaya, chief manager of Toho’s animation division and planning group leader.
	

	The award’s name and outline will be revealed Nov. 2 at the closing event of Tokyo Anime Next, the festival that organized the session. Co-hosted by the AJA and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, Tokyo Anime Next runs Oct. 30–Nov. 2 in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro district, with several events at TIFFCOM.

	The 2027 launch date has yet to be confirmed, and the panelists stressed that their views were not the award’s official positions.

	“Creators should be highlighted – and they should be put in the limelight,” Shimizu said when asked about the timing of the launch.

	Saito Masaya said Toho had helped work on the concept for the award, and agreed that creators should be highlighted. He added that the award could give fans a more direct connection to the people behind anime’s global popularity. The company wants to “help achieve a wider reach to anime fans and help give them a wider perspective,” he said, bringing them closer to different creative styles and approaches.
	

	Saito Yuichiro, a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, said an award is only one part of what the Academy does. “There are many different branches of work beyond the award,” he said. “The Academy Award in the United States is a domestic award, but it now has a global membership. They also provide training, and try to create a sort of succession plan for the industry. This kind of philosophy is the backbone for the award.”

	Ideally, the panelists said, financial support and training would also be among the building blocks of the new award.

	Saito Masaya said he hoped the award “can contribute to the changing of the ways audience enjoy anime.” He wants fans “to notice a certain aspect and ask who is behind this,” he added.

	Shimizu said the need to showcase the value of Japanese animation was “one of the key phrases.” “Japanese anime has a very unique workflow and processes, so who does what and who evaluates what, and who delivers those, and how are they embraced and valued by the audience,” he said.

	The panel noted that some awards have already picked up on that uniqueness. The Annie Awards have added a best international anime production for TV/media category for their 54th edition.

	“Japanese anime is a standalone established category,” Shimizu said, “anime is different from Disney, it is different from Pixar.”

	He said the new award should reflect those differences by spotlighting the creators who work on each part of an anime’s production. “For a layperson, the beauty of the anime can’t be expressed clearly in words,” he said.

	Saito Yuichiro said the world has two major trends. “The first one is this European Art History, generated from that long history and value system, and the worldwide large-scale trends centered in the United States. The world is composed of these two systems,” he said.

	He asked whether Asia could build its own equivalent “aesthetics and value system,” and whether an awards body could help bring an Asian voice into a system he sees as dominated by Europe and the U.S.

	“Borderlessness is very important, what I’d hope is to blur the boundaries between these areas of the world with these awards,” he said.

title: Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’
description: Known for her dark relationship dramas, including the 2017 multiple-award-winner “Dear Etranger,” Mishima Yukiko has taken a different approach wit
body:
Known for her dark relationship dramas, including the 2017 multiple-award-winner “Dear Etranger,” Mishima Yukiko has taken a different approach with her latest film, “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights,” which is in competition at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival.

	Based on a 2014 novel by Chihaya Akane, it stars Matsuoka Mayu as Kanna, a picture book illustrator who has tired of her nice-but-boring live-in boyfriend (Inoue Yuki) while having nothing but a physical connection with her cynical married lover (Nakajima Ayumu).
	

	Then a close friend from her college days, Haseo (Narita Ryo), reenters her life after a gap of seven years and once again becomes her confidant. Now a salesman for a drug company and still single, Haseo is something of a womanizer, though he keeps his relationship with Kanna strictly platonic.

	Shot in Kyoto, Hiroshima and Toyama Prefecture, the film makes screenwriter Sawai Kaori’s talky script feel visually dynamic, while avoiding cliché shots in Kyoto and Hiroshima, two of Japan’s most famous tourist destinations. Instead of posing against temples and cherry blossoms, the two principals stroll along a riverbank or on railroad tracks as they renew their friendship – and flirt with something more.

	“When deciding on a location, it’s not just about picking a ‘pretty’ spot,” says Mishima in an interview at Tokyo Midtown, the main festival site. “Rather it’s more about choosing a place where the scene comes to life.”

	“Also, the novel has a lot of scenes set inside a coffee shop, but in the movie (Kanna and Haseo) are walking just about the whole time,” she adds.
	

	Years ago, she and a male friend spent more time walking together than sitting inside a shop and talking, she recalls. “We didn’t talk about our worries and troubles – we’d walk until dawn, just chatting about trivial things.”

	“Trivial” is not the word to describe the film’s dialogue, but it has a bantering tone, as well as an unfiltered honesty.

	At the same time, Kanna and Haseo don’t face each other right away. “I didn’t want them to do that until a certain point,” says Mishima. “I wanted them to always be looking in the same direction. So when they go into a ramen shop, they are sitting side by side at a counter. The same with buses and trains – they sit next to each other, looking in the same direction.”

	A big influence in her shotmaking style, Mishima says, is Ozu Yasujiro, who often filmed characters side by side or even making the same motions in unison. “I love how he captures the way people move within the flow of Japanese life, without cutting the shot, creating a sense of wonder,” she says. “He is also brilliant in how he makes a grand narrative emerge from small, personal moments, so I’ve been greatly influenced by that as well. My film starts from that personal perspective, but then it kind of opens up to the world.”

	The film’s first act hints at sex comedy, and Mishima cast both of her leads – Matsuoka (“Tremble All You Want”) and Narita (“Convenience Story”) – with their comic abilities in mind. But she has crafted something more intimate and complex, with an ending open to interpretation.

	“I thought that having a good sense for comedy was essential for the long dialogue scenes,” says Mishima. “They require a sense of rhythm and actors with a feel for comedy have it. It makes a huge difference.”

	The film is no lighthearted laugh fest: Kanna and Haseo are not always likable characters, acting in ways selfish, callous and even cruel. “I think movies should be able to portray all kinds of people and tell all kinds of stories,” says Mishima. “And it’s good to have characters that represent all kinds of people, too.”

	“I think viewers will probably be able to relate to their emotions,” she adds. “They’ll be able to find a part of themselves – ‘Oh, I’ve felt this way too.’ That’s what makes a good actor. No matter how bad the person they’re portraying is, you end up understanding them or rather you can’t help but feel the way they do. That’s their charm.”
	

	Other characters add their perspectives, such as a surly bartender who is close to Haseo and thinks Kanna is hurting him, and Kanna’s jaded college friend who freely admits to cheating on her husband and sympathizes with Kanna’s infidelities. “I wanted to present the story in a multi-layered way,” says Mishima. “The film’s Japanese title is ‘The Male Friend,’ but it gradually drifts away from that theme. It’s more a story about what Kanna comes to see. By spending time with Haseo, she gains a perspective that lets her see not just herself but the world.”

	Kanna’s art also changes. In sharp contrast to the commercial hack work that pays her bills, she completes a painting that grows out of her three eventful days with Haseo. “What I want to convey is embedded in that final painting,” says Mishima. “Kanna learns something in Hiroshima about herself and the world and puts that message into her painting. I wanted to depict the whole process, right up to the point where viewers come to see her painting and receive that message.”

schema.headline: Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’

title: Sourav Ganguly’s ‘Bigg Boss Bangla’ Among Highlights as Indian Media Giant JioStar Revenues Climb 10%
description: JioStar, the Indian media giant backed by Reliance Industries, grew revenue from operations 10.1% year-on-year to INR68.1 billion ($710 million) in
body:
JioStar, the Indian media giant backed by Reliance Industries, grew revenue from operations 10.1% year-on-year to INR68.1 billion ($710 million) in the July–September quarter despite a weak advertising market. Profit after tax fell 13.2% to INR11.5 billion ($120 million).

	Former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly hosted the first-ever “Bigg Boss Bangla,” which launched this quarter on streaming service JioHotstar. The reality franchise rolled out in six languages, and all editions together pulled in more than 90 million viewers in their first three weeks. That makes “Bigg Boss” the biggest entertainment property on the platform.
	

	Reliance Industries credited JioStar’s revenue growth to subscriptions and to advertising on digital entertainment. Gross revenue rose 9.8% to INR79.4 billion ($829 million).

	Margins came under pressure. EBITDA from operations dropped 10.5% to INR13.7 billion ($143 million), and the margin fell to 22.1% from 28.1% a year earlier. A 36.6% drop in investment income pulled total EBITDA down 13.6% to INR15 billion ($157 million). The quarter was also well below April–June, when JioStar booked INR109.5 billion ($1.1 billion) in revenue from operations.

	JioHotstar averaged about 440 million monthly active users over the three months, up 10% on the prior year. In September, the platform relaunched under the JioHotstar name in the U.K., Canada and Singapore. Reliance said active subscribers in those three territories have grown about 30% since then.

	The company also introduced “Pay Kisi Aur Se” (“Ask Others to Pay”), which lets users send a subscription payment request to a friend or relative. Reliance said the feature raised payment initiations by 10%. Subscribers on mobile plans now get up to two hours a month of viewing on connected TVs. The average JioHotstar viewer on a connected TV watches three times as much as one on a phone.
	

	Watch time for entertainment content grew more than 15%, with Hindi and regional markets performing well. Reliance said titles including “India Ke Top 1%,” “Khatron Ke Khiladi,” “Hustle” Season 5 and “Bhojpuri Bawaal” strengthened JioStar’s position as the country’s top entertainment network.

	“Resort” became the most-watched title in the streamer’s history, which Reliance cited as evidence that its bet on long-running series is paying off. Rajkumar Hirani’s “Pritam & Pedro” set the platform record for a short-running series. “Heart Beat” Season 3 and new series “Court” both opened strongly, and Hindi drama “Thukra Ke Mera Pyaar” Season 2 improved on its first season. Tadka also grew its catalog, adding nearly 100 titles spanning reality, sports and other categories.

	In sports, the England–India cricket series gave JioHotstar its biggest audience yet for a bilateral series played abroad. Wimbledon, the U.S. Open and the opening weeks of the 2026–27 Premier League season drew steady audiences and were monetized more effectively, according to the company. JioStar also expanded its commerce integrations, which had been limited to cricket, to all three events.

	The results came two days after Jio Platforms, Reliance’s separate telecom and digital arm, listed on Indian stock exchanges. Reliance said the INR301.9 billion ($3.15 billion) IPO is the largest in India to date. Mukesh Ambani, Reliance’s chairman and managing director, said the issue was subscribed more than 22 times.

schema.headline: Sourav Ganguly’s ‘Bigg Boss Bangla’ Among Highlights as Indian Media Giant JioStar Revenues Climb 10%

title: Ranbir Kapoor, Yash Light Up Gold House’s Diwali Event as Group Launches South Asian Shorts Fund
description: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, stars of the epic adaptation “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” opened Gold House’s largest Gold Diwali to date at The Majestic
body:
Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, stars of the epic adaptation “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” opened Gold House’s largest Gold Diwali to date at The Majestic Downtown in Los Angeles, alongside filmmakers Nitesh Tiwari and Namit Malhotra, a week before the film’s release.

	Gold House, which works to back and celebrate the Asian Pacific community, staged the gathering ahead of Diwali, which falls on Nov. 8 this year. The organization pitched “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” as the biggest film ever produced out of India. Based on the ancient epic, it opens worldwide on Nov. 5, and a DJ set and dance floor themed around the movie ran through the night.
	

	The group also used the evening to unveil the Gold Stack Shorts Fund, a partnership with South Stack Studios that will support proof-of-concept shorts and micro-series built on South Asian stories. Submissions are open through Nov. 30, with the chosen projects to be named Jan. 10, before Sundance.

	“Diwali is a celebration of light, community and connection, and we wanted to bring that spirit to our Gold Diwali while honoring how culture shapes who we are and the possibilities we create,” said Bing Chen, Gold House’s executive chair and CEO.

	Indian luxury designer Anita Dongre debuted a one-off carrom board, painted by hand in collaboration with Gold House, that recasts the tabletop game common in South Asian homes as a contemporary design object. Guests also saw the Cuyana x Gold House Marigold Charm, a limited-edition piece released earlier in October.

	Co-hosts spanned entertainment, media, fashion and business. Among them were Tan France, Freida Pinto, Avantika, Sarayu Blue, Dhar Mann, Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash, Poshmark chairman Manish Chandra and Kabir Ahuja, McKinsey’s global head of TMT and consumer technology. Anita Dongre and Yash Dongre were also among the co-hosts, as was South Stack Studios.
	

	The guest list included Saheli Khan, Aishu Devan and Sehaj Sethi of “Avatar: Seven Havens,” along with Hannah Simone, Janina Gavankar, Manish Dayal, Sanya Malhotra, Richa Moorjani, Nisha Ganatra, Asif Ali, Michelle Khare and Avani Gregg.

	Rasoi Catering served regional South Asian dishes, and a lounge was set aside for carrom. DJ MissNinja shared the music with KVS Tabla, an act that fuses tabla with electronic music and other styles. Bhindi Jewelers hosted a jewelry experience, while dating app Dil Mil sponsored a portrait station produced by The Lounge Booth. Smartwater, Glance, McKinsey & Company and Google’s 100 Zeros also backed the event, which was produced by BMF Productions.

	In remarks during the night, Chen said Gold Diwali was not just for the Festival of Lights. “It’s for the creators, founders, and true builders who know that shining, that overnight success, is decades in the making,” he said.

	The party follows the recent rollout of Gold House’s Diwali Cultural Guide.

schema.headline: Ranbir Kapoor, Yash Light Up Gold House’s Diwali Event as Group Launches South Asian Shorts Fund

title: How Keanu Reeves Landed in Stop-Motion Samurai Epic ‘Hidari’ – and Why S.S. Rajamouli Wanted to Know How It Was Made
description: Keanu Reeves joined Japanese stop-motion feature “Hidari” after watching the project’s pilot film, with his team getting back to the filmmakers abo
body:
Keanu Reeves joined Japanese stop-motion feature “Hidari” after watching the project’s pilot film, with his team getting back to the filmmakers about a week after the screening was arranged to set up a Zoom call, director Kawamura Masashi said at the Tokyo International Film Festival, where he also updated the film’s fundraising push.

	Kawamura, who created, wrote and is directing “Hidari,” appeared with co-director Ogawa Iku at a session reporting on Film Frontier, a talent development program backed by Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs and run by festival organizer UniJapan. The program has paid for the team’s travel to markets and industry events.
	

	Reeves’ casting as the lead voice was announced at Cannes in May, but Kawamura said the actor had seen the pilot before the festival.

	“We were heavily influenced by Kurosawa’s films, so when the puppet was being made, I asked for Mifune Toshiro and Keanu Reeves added together, divided by two and then aged,” Kawamura said.

	From then on, Kawamura kept Reeves at the top of his list for the lead voice. The film’s producers took that seriously, found a way to reach the actor and arranged for him to watch the pilot.

	“About a week later we heard back, and it was, ‘OK, let’s do a Zoom,’” Kawamura said. “I was thinking, so this is how fast things move these days. Then we got on the call and Keanu was there on the other side.”

	“Hidari” has also caught the eye of “RRR” director S.S. Rajamouli. Kawamura said he met the Indian filmmaker at Annecy, showed him “Hidari” and ended up in a standing conversation of about 30 minutes about how the film was made.
	

	“He said, ‘You’re amazing. How did you make this?’” Kawamura said.

	Kawamura said an encounter like that, with a director he would rarely cross paths with otherwise, could only happen at a festival. “There’s the surprise inside the theater, and there are the connections after you walk out,” he said.

	The team shot the proof-of-concept short around three years ago, paying for it themselves with help from crowdfunding, and posted it on YouTube. It has since drawn about 5.3 million views and roughly 120,000 followers, many of them overseas, according to Kawamura.

	“Wood carving, stop-motion and a period drama – it’s a very austere project,” he said. “If we’d pitched it with just a written proposal, I don’t think anyone would have understood it.”

	With Film Frontier support, the filmmakers pitched “Hidari” at the Annecy Animation Showcase, part of the Cannes Film Market, carrying one of the hand-carved puppets with them. Kawamura said the puppet drew bigger crowds than its makers, and the Cannes platform put the film in front of live-action and action fans as well as distributors and agents.

	“Stop-motion is a really small world, and people tend to assume it’s a narrow market,” Kawamura said. “But even though it’s stop-motion, we think of it as an action film.”

	The budget is large, and the team is still out selling the project, seeking grants and partnerships with overseas distributors, Kawamura said. “In terms of speed, we’re making it the indie way,” he added. “Thanks to being light on our feet, I think the project has managed to make it across thin ice.”

	Earlier this month in Busan, Dwarf Studios producer Matsumoto Noriko said talks with a U.S. company that had offered to fund the entire budget, in exchange for all the rights, had stalled.

	Ogawa, who works at stop-motion house Dwarf Studios, attended Annecy this year. He said the technique remains niche in commercial film and TV animation, but festival shorts and student sections are full of it, and studios from Europe, North America and beyond converge on Annecy. “When I took the puppet along, it was hugely popular,” he said. “It was fun.”

	Film Frontier, now in its third year, is part of the Agency for Cultural Affairs’ Creator Support Fund, which backs creators for around three years, from project development through to overseas rollout.

schema.headline: How Keanu Reeves Landed in Stop-Motion Samurai Epic ‘Hidari’ – and Why S.S. Rajamouli Wanted to Know How It Was Made

title: Georgia’s ‘Guria’ Wins Best Film at Asia Pacific Screen Awards as Thailand’s Sompot Chidgasornpongse Takes Director Prize
description: Georgian filmmaker Levan Koguashvili’s “Guria” was named best film at the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards, handed out Oct. 30 at The Star Gold Coas
body:
Georgian filmmaker Levan Koguashvili’s “Guria” was named best film at the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards, handed out Oct. 30 at The Star Gold Coast in Queensland, Australia.

	Koguashvili shared the prize with fellow producers Olena Yershova and Boris Frumin. The film was made across seven countries: Georgia, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Norway and Saudi Arabia.


	Thai director Sompot Chidgasornpongse won best director for “9 Temples to Heaven,” a co-production involving Thailand, Singapore, France, Norway, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia and Qatar. Myanmar’s Aung Phyoe received a special mention in the directing category for “Fruit Gathering.” Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat took the Jury Grand Prize for “No Good Men.”
	

	This year’s field comprised 36 nominated films from 32 countries and regions.

	Nepalese actor Pushpa Thing Lama won best performance for “Elephants in the Fog,” and South Korea’s Sim Su-bin was named best new performer for “The World Before.” The screenplay award went to Rakan Mayasi, Wahid Ajmi and Pôl Seif for “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep,” backed by Belgium, Lebanon, Palestine, Qatar and Saudi Arabia. Vietnamese cinematographer Nguyễn Vinh Phúc won for “Hearing.”

	New Zealand’s Paloma Schneideman took best youth film for “Big Girls Don’t Cry,” produced by Vicky Pope and Thomas Coppell. The animation prize went to “The Violinist,” a co-production between Singapore, Spain and Italy that was co-directed by Singapore’s Ervin Han and Spain’s Raúl García.
	

	Itab Azzam and Jack MacInness won best documentary for “One in a Million,” a U.K.-U.S. film that follows the life of a Syrian refugee. Isabelle Kalandar, who both directed and produced “Another Birth,” received the Cultural Diversity Award for the Tajikistan, U.S. and Qatar collaboration. India’s R. Gowtham earned the Young Cinema Award, given with NETPAC, for “Members of the Problematic Family.”

	Malaysian filmmaker Haziqah Azemi won the Forum Filmmaker Award, run with The Post Lounge Group, for her project “Garek.” The story centers on a woman whose relationship is tested when she faces religious persecution after becoming pregnant outside marriage. Azemi, who took part in the Griffith Film School and APSA Regional Reels program, came back to APSA this year after developing the project with mentoring from APSA Academy member Yulia Evina Bhara.

	Tracey Vieira, chair of the Asia Pacific Screen Awards, said: “From ‘Guria’ and ‘No Good Men’ to ‘Elephants in the Fog,’ this year’s winners remind us of the extraordinary stories emerging from our region and the importance of creating opportunities for these voices to be recognized internationally.”

	Veteran Indian producer Bobby Bedi was handed the FIAPF Award for outstanding contribution to film in the Asia Pacific. Luis Alberto Scalella, president of FIAPF, said: “Through landmark films such as ‘Bandit Queen’ and ‘Fire,’ he has championed powerful stories that have challenged audiences and resonated far beyond India.”

	The ceremony also revealed five projects selected for the 2026 MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, each of which will get a $10,000 grant funded entirely by the Motion Picture Association. They are Payal Kapadia’s “A Memory of Being Here” (India), produced by Thomas Hakim; Davy Chou’s “My Father’s Glory” (France, Cambodia), produced by Charlotte Vincent; Taifeng Liu’s “A Place in the Sun” (China), produced by Janet (Yan Yan) Wu; Nicole Midori Woodford’s “Incarnation” (Singapore, Japan), produced by Anthony Chen; and Zhanana Kurmasheva’s documentary “The Story of My Shirt” (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China, Chile), produced by Banu Ramazanova.

	Three of the five projects are directed by women. Chen returns to the fund after working on “We Are All Strangers,” which received a grant in 2023 and was among this year’s nominees.
	

	Urmila Venugopalan, president and managing director, Asia Pacific, at the Motion Picture Association, said the success of films such as “9 Temples to Heaven,” which received MPA APSA Academy Film Fund support in 2021, “shows the importance of supporting filmmakers and their stories from the earliest stages of development.”

	Every APSA nominee, along with members of the nominations councils and juries, joins the APSA Academy, whose president is Australian screen veteran Jack Thompson. The body now has upward of 1,816 members across 84 countries and areas.

	The full list of winners:

	Best Film“Guria,” dir. Levan Koguashvili; prod. Olena Yershova, Levan Koguashvili, Boris Frumin (Georgia, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Norway, Saudi Arabia)

	Jury Grand PrizeShahrbanoo Sadat, “No Good Men” (Germany, France, Norway, Denmark, Afghanistan)

	Best DirectorSompot Chidgasornpongse, “9 Temples to Heaven” (Thailand, Singapore, France, Norway, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Qatar)

	Best Director – Special MentionAung Phyoe, “Fruit Gathering” (Myanmar, Czech Republic, France)

	Best Youth Film“Big Girls Don’t Cry,” dir. Paloma Schneideman; prod. Vicky Pope, Thomas Coppell (New Zealand)

	Best Animated Film“The Violinist,” dir. Ervin Han, Raúl García; prod. Paloma Mora, Cristiano Bortone, Justin Deimen, Leonard Lai, Takafumi Yuki (Singapore, Spain, Italy)

	Best Documentary Film“One in a Million,” dir. Itab Azzam, Jack MacInness; prod. Itab Azzam, Jack MacInness, Will Anderson, James Bluemel, Andrew Palmer, Raney Aronson-Rath (U.K., U.S.)

	Best ScreenplayRakan Mayasi, Wahid Ajmi, Pôl Seif, “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep” (Belgium, Lebanon, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia)

	Best CinematographyNguyễn Vinh Phúc, “Hearing” (Vietnam, Singapore, Norway, France, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Cambodia, Thailand, Taiwan)

	Best PerformancePushpa Thing Lama, “Elephants in the Fog” (Nepal, Germany, Brazil, France, Norway)

	Best New PerformerSim Su-bin, “The World Before” (South Korea)

	Cultural Diversity Award“Another Birth,” dir./prod. Isabelle Kalandar (Tajikistan, U.S., Qatar)

	Young Cinema Award (in partnership with Netpac)R. Gowtham, “Members of the Problematic Family” (India)
	

	FIAPF AwardBobby Bedi (India)

	Forum Filmmaker AwardHaziqah Azemi, “Garek” (Malaysia)

	MPA APSA Academy Film Fund“A Memory of Being Here,” dir. Payal Kapadia; prod. Thomas Hakim (India)“My Father’s Glory,” dir. Davy Chou; prod. Charlotte Vincent (France, Cambodia)“A Place in the Sun,” dir. Taifeng Liu; prod. Janet (Yan Yan) Wu (China)“Incarnation,” dir. Nicole Midori Woodford; prod. Anthony Chen (Singapore, Japan)“The Story of My Shirt,” dir. Zhanana Kurmasheva; prod. Banu Ramazanova (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China, Chile)

title: General Hospital's Steve Burton: Read Alleged Texts From Fight With Ex Over Kid Going to Emmys
description:
'General Hospital' Steve Burton
                          Read Alleged Texts From Fight Over Kid Going
body:
'General Hospital' Steve Burton
                          Read Alleged Texts From Fight Over Kid Going to Emmys ...
                          Ex Disgusted By 'Hollywood Scene'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 31, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            "General Hospital" star Steve Burton's ex-wife, Sheree Gustin, allegedly told him she would not allow their daughter to go to the Emmys because she didn't want the kid near the "Hollywood scene" ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            In court docs, obtained by TMZ, Steve complained about his ex's recent decision to deny his request to take their 12-year-old daughter Brooklyn to the Daytime Emmys ... which are going down today.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve claimed his ex refused to allow him to swap days, despite him being nominated at the awards.
      
    
            In alleged texts submitted to the court and obtained by TMZ, Steve wrote, "I would like Brook there. Let me know. Thanks. I would pick her up Friday morning and take her back Saturday."
      

            Per the docs, Sheree said, "That doesn’t work," which prompted the soap star to reply, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime. I'll be happy to swap days."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sheree allegedly responded, "Once in a lifetime lol? I don't want Brooklyn anywhere near Hollywood or that scene. You plaster her on social media and People magazine enough. Absolutely not."
      
    
            In the alleged exchange, Steve said, "Yes. I'm nominated and would like the girls with me," adding, "For years you were perfectly comfortable with the lifestyle that came from my career in that world. And even now, your whole business is built from social media, which includes Brooklyn a lot. And it's not about us plastering Brooklyn all over Hollywood. I'm nominated, and I would love for her to be there with us."
      
    
            It doesn't appear Sheree responded to the text.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Steve and Sheree have been going back and forth for months about their daughter Brooklyn, including a dispute as to whether she should live in California or Tennessee.
      
    
            Steve and Sheree were married for 23 years before splitting in 2022.
